An Australian lawmaker said she was "full of gratitude" as she was discharged from hospital on Monday following an alleged attack in October that resulted in her losing both legs.

Independent politician Helen Haines was struck outside her office in rural Australia, suffering serious injuries that eventually led to the amputation of her legs.

The attack has sparked much soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare but where police have documented a steady rise in threats towards elected officials.

The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said the 65-year-old had been discharged four weeks after she was airlifted in for emergency treatment.

"I am very pleased to confirm that I have moved into the rehabilitation stage of my recovery, which will continue in Melbourne for the immediate future," she said in a statement.

"This is a really positive moment and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage."

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he was in regular contact with Haines and her family and wished her the best for her recovery.

"We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation," he said in a statement.

Haines was standing near her car in the rural Australian town of Wangaratta when she was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser on 19 October.

Police have charged 43-year-old Brendan Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, as well as the federal crime of harming a public official.

Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as cracking down on corruption and stronger climate action.

O rachetă Vulcan, operată de United Launch Alliance (ULA), companie deținută în comun de Boeing și Lockheed Martin, a eșuat duminică, la aproximativ 10 minute după lansarea de la baza spațială Cape Canaveral din Florida. Incidentul a dus la pierderea celor 40 de sateliți Amazon Leo transportați la bord, care nu au mai putut fi plasați pe orbită. Este primul eșec al unei misiuni spațiale din istoria de 20 de ani a ULA.

Potrivit companiei, racheta a suferit o anomalie în timpul zborului, însă cauza exactă nu este deocamdată cunoscută. ULA a anunțat că va analiza datele primite în timpul lansării pentru a stabili ce a provocat incidentul. Investigația tehnică ar putea dura mai multe luni, perioadă în care racheta Vulcan ar putea fi ținută la sol.

Eșecul reprezintă o lovitură atât pentru ULA, care încearcă să transforme Vulcan în principala sa rachetă pentru lansări comerciale și militare, cât și pentru Amazon, care depinde de furnizori externi pentru construirea propriei rețele de internet prin satelit, numită Leo.

Lansarea de duminică era prima dintr-o serie de misiuni prin care ULA urma să transporte în mod regulat sateliți Amazon pe orbită. Compania americană încearcă să dezvolte o rețea care să concureze cu Starlink, serviciul de internet prin satelit al SpaceX, însă programul său a fost întârziat în repetate rânduri de problemele întâmpinate de companiile care asigură lansările.

Amazon avea, înainte de incident, 398 de sateliți Leo pe orbită, plasați în urma a 14 lansări începute în 2025. Numărul reprezenta aproximativ 12% din cei 3.236 de sateliți de care compania estimează că are nevoie pentru a asigura acoperire globală. Amazon spera să înceapă furnizarea primelor servicii de internet în cursul acestui an.

Incidentul ar putea agrava problemele cu care se confruntă industria americană a lansărilor spațiale. Dacă Vulcan va rămâne la sol pentru mai multe luni, numărul rachetelor disponibile pentru transportul sateliților și al altor încărcături în spațiu va fi și mai redus.

Situația este complicată și de problemele întâmpinate de alți furnizori, precum Blue Origin, dar și de incertitudinile privind disponibilitatea rachetei Falcon 9 a SpaceX, cea mai utilizată rachetă din lume. Reuters notează că SpaceX nu mai acceptă în prezent rezervări pentru noi lansări Falcon 9.

În plus, Forțele Spațiale ale SUA nu aprobaseră încă reluarea lansărilor de sateliți militari cu Vulcan, după problemele tehnice înregistrate la zborurile precedente. Misiunea de duminică urma să ofere date suplimentare înainte ca armata americană să decidă dacă racheta poate fi folosită din nou pentru transportul încărcăturilor de securitate națională.

United Launch Alliance a fost înființată în 2006, prin fuziunea programelor de rachete Delta, dezvoltate de Boeing, și Atlas, dezvoltate de Lockheed Martin. Până la incidentul de duminică, compania avea un istoric de 100% misiuni reușite, ceea ce face ca eșecul să fie unul deosebit de important pentru reputația sa.

A good night's sleep does more than ease yesterday's fatigue. As the body rests, the brain drives processes that build muscle, fortify bones, burn fat and sharpen thinking on waking.

Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have identified the neural circuit that regulates the release of growth hormone during sleep, in a study published in the scientific journal "Cell". Their findings show that the relationship between sleep and growth hormone is not, as commonly assumed, a one-way street: sleep promotes the secretion of this hormone, while growth hormone in turn helps regulate when we wake up.

Scientists have long known that a significant amount of growth hormone is released during sleep. Beyond its central role in height gain in children and adolescents, this hormone continues in adulthood to help preserve muscle tissue, keep bones healthy, regulate the use of stored fat and control blood sugar levels.

Until now, however, it was unclear exactly how the brain regulates the release of this hormone across different sleep stages, and how neural activity, growth hormone levels and the timing of awakening are connected.

Xinlu Ding, a postdoctoral researcher in neuroscience at Berkeley and the study’s lead author, explains that scientists previously examined the link between sleep and growth hormone mainly by measuring hormone levels in the blood. In the new research, by contrast, they directly recorded the activity of nerve cells in the brains of mice.

According to Ding, this approach enabled the team to pinpoint a specific neural circuit that could serve as a basis for investigating future treatments.

How does the brain control growth hormone release during sleep?

To find the answer, the researchers focused on a part of the brain called the hypothalamus – a small but vital region involved in regulating hunger, body temperature, hormone production and the sleep–wake cycle.

In this area of the brain, one group of nerve cells produces growth hormone–releasing hormone, or GHRH, which stimulates the secretion of growth hormone. Another group produces somatostatin, which has an inhibitory effect. The interplay between these two chemical messengers fine-tunes the amount of growth hormone released by the pituitary gland into the bloodstream.

The scientists found that the activity of these cells is not the same across different stages of sleep.

During non-REM sleep – the phase that makes up much of the body’s deep, restorative sleep – the activity of somatostatin-producing cells drops, weakening their inhibitory effect. At the same time, the cells linked to GHRH become somewhat more active, creating favourable conditions for increased growth hormone release.

In REM sleep, the stage usually associated with vivid dreaming, the pattern shifts again. Activity related to both messengers rises and, despite their seemingly opposite roles, the precise coordination of neural activity in this phase further boosts growth hormone secretion.

In other words, the researchers have shown that the brain can draw on different neural pathways in different sleep stages to regulate the release of a single essential hormone.

How does growth hormone influence waking up?

Perhaps the most striking result of the study is that growth hormone is not simply a by-product of what the brain does during sleep; it also feeds back on the neural circuits that govern wakefulness.

The team discovered that as growth hormone levels rise during sleep, they stimulate the activity of nerve cells in an area of the brainstem known as the "locus coeruleus". This region plays a key role in alertness, attention, concentration and preparing the brain to respond to its surroundings.

Put simply, sleep increases growth hormone secretion, and the rise in growth hormone then signals to the brain that it is time to move towards wakefulness. The scientists describe this as a feedback loop that helps maintain balance between sleep, hormone release and alertness.

Daniel Silverman, a co-author of the study and postdoctoral researcher at Berkeley, says the findings show that sleep and growth hormone form part of a highly delicate regulatory system: inadequate sleep can reduce growth hormone secretion, while rising hormone levels in turn nudge the brain towards waking.

Maintaining this balance, he adds, is crucial for growth, tissue repair and healthy metabolism.

The researchers also highlight an unexpected observation. Although increased activity in the locus coeruleus usually makes us more alert, overstimulating the nerve cells in this region can have the opposite effect and lead to drowsiness rather than wakefulness.

This suggests that healthy brain function does not simply depend on ramping up or shutting down a single group of neurons, but on a finely tuned equilibrium between multiple signals.

Linking poor sleep to obesity, diabetes and brain disorders

The study’s findings may shed new light on the connection between insufficient sleep and certain metabolic disorders.

Growth hormone helps regulate fat use and blood sugar levels, and chronic sleep disruption can upset the balance of its secretion. Lack of sleep may therefore be one factor that increases the risk of obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, even though these conditions also have many other causes.

The researchers also suspect that the link between growth hormone and brain regions responsible for alertness and concentration could have consequences beyond physical health.

Xinlu Ding notes that, in addition to supporting the building and maintenance of muscles and bones and regulating fat tissue, growth hormone may have a positive effect on cognitive performance, improving a person’s level of alertness after waking.

According to the team, identifying this neural circuit could eventually pave the way for new treatments for sleep disorders associated with metabolic diseases and neurological conditions such as Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s.

Even so, the scientists stress that their experiments were carried out on mice, and it is not yet clear whether the mechanism works in exactly the same way in humans. Further research will be needed to assess whether these insights can be translated into therapies.

The results therefore do not prove that a new sleeping technique can help people lose weight or build muscle. Instead, they represent a step towards understanding the mechanisms that tie these processes to sleep.

Ultimately, the Berkeley team’s work is a reminder that sleep, despite its calm outward appearance, is a period of intense, finely choreographed activity in the brain and body – a time when nerve cells and hormones constantly communicate to keep growth, repair, metabolism and wakefulness in balance.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote on X that the GRU had ordered a "sabotage attempt" at the Estonian defence company Threod Systems on Saturday night.

Estonia said on Sunday it would close its border with Russia after stopping what it called an attempted arson attack by Russia's GRU military intelligence on a drone factory.

The move marked a sharp escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia, which Tallinn sees as part of a broader campaign of hostile activity linked to Moscow's war against Ukraine.

"Estonia will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of 1 December," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote in a post on X, citing "clear evidence" that the GRU had ordered the attack.

Moscow said it would verify whether Estonia was indeed planning to shut all crossings.

"We will verify all this to see if it's true," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told the TASS news agency.

"But if these are their (Estonia's) real plans, then it will be seen as yet another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia," she added.

Earlier on Sunday, Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote on X that the GRU had ordered a "sabotage attempt" at the Estonian defence company Threod Systems on Saturday night.

"Extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures and a swift reaction by law enforcement. The attackers have been detained," he added.

The foiled attack happened in Viimsi, north of the capital Tallinn.

Tsahkna, in his later post, said: "Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences.

"Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered."

He also said he had informed his Finnish, Latvian, and Lithuanian counterparts of the decision.

Security forces arrested eight individuals who live in Latvia, chief prosecutor Astrid Asi told journalists.

Michal called the incident "part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia".

"We will not be intimidated," he added.

Threod Systems manufactures reconnaissance and attack drones.

In August, the defence subcontractor Milrem Robotics, based in Tallinn, was targeted in an attempted arson attack and Latvian nationals were arrested.

Estonia, a member of the European Union and NATO, currently has three crossing points with Russia at Narva in the north and the southern Luhamaa and Koidula crossing, that allow the movement of people and goods between the two countries.

Russia suspended vehicle traffic through Narva in February 2024, although pedestrians were still allowed to pass.

The crossings are among the few remaining overland links between Russia and the European Union still operating since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Președintele american Donald Trump se întâlnește săptămâna aceasta cu liderul chinez Xi Jinping (dar și cu Vladimir Putin), în condițiile în care Washingtonul nu a reușit încă să-și construiască propriile surse de aprovizionare cu minerale critice, esențiale pentru industria semiconductorilor, producția de automobile electrice, robotică, inteligență artificială și echipamente militare. Dependența de China îi limitează astfel capacitatea de negociere, deoarece Beijingul poate folosi controlul asupra acestor materii prime ca instrument de presiune în disputele comerciale.

Deși Administrația Trump a investit miliarde de dolari în proiecte miniere și de procesare a mineralelor, multe dintre acestea sunt încă departe de a începe producția. Reconstruirea unei industrii pe care Statele Unite au abandonat-o în mare parte spre sfârșitul secolului trecut este un proces dificil, care necesită ani de investiții, infrastructură și dezvoltarea unor tehnologii specializate.

China deține o poziție dominantă nu doar în extracția pământurilor rare, ci mai ales în procesarea acestora și fabricarea componentelor industriale rezultate. Un exemplu relevant este producția de magneți permanenți din neodim și fier, utilizați în motoarele automobilelor electrice și în echipamentele militare. În 2025, capacitatea de producție a Statelor Unite era de aproximativ 4.500 de tone anual, în timp ce China putea produce circa 210.000 de tone.

Această diferență îi oferă Beijingului un avantaj important în negocieri. În 2025, după ce China a impus restricții asupra exporturilor de pământuri rare și magneți, mai mulți producători americani au întâmpinat dificultăți în aprovizionare. Ford a avertizat că are probleme în obținerea magneților necesari producției, iar Washingtonul a fost nevoit să negocieze cu Beijingul pentru restabilirea accesului la aceste materiale.

Disputa privind pământurile rare a fost unul dintre subiectele centrale ale războiului comercial dintre Statele Unite și China. În mai 2025, cele două țări au convenit, la Geneva, asupra unui armistițiu tarifar de 90 de zile, care prevedea și suspendarea unor măsuri comerciale restrictive. Ulterior, în iunie, negocierile de la Londra au dus la un nou cadru de înțelegere, prin care China s-a angajat să reia exporturile de pământuri rare și magneți permanenți către Statele Unite.

În octombrie 2025, Beijingul a anunțat noi restricții, inclusiv asupra unor produse fabricate în alte țări care conțin materiale rare provenite din China. Măsurile au fost suspendate în urma întâlnirii dintre Trump și Xi Jinping de la Busan, din 30 octombrie 2025, când cei doi lideri au convenit asupra unui nou armistițiu comercial. În schimbul unor concesii americane, China a acceptat să suspende timp de un an extinderea restricțiilor la export.

Cu toate acestea, acordurile nu au eliminat sistemul chinez de autorizare a exporturilor, ceea ce înseamnă că Beijingul păstrează controlul asupra cantităților și destinațiilor livrărilor. Datele privind comerțul arată că aprovizionarea americană nu și-a revenit la nivelurile de dinaintea restricțiilor. În perioada iunie 2024 – martie 2025, Statele Unite importau din China, în medie, 76,8 tone pe lună de compuși și metale din pământuri rare. În cele 11 luni de după acordul de la Busan, între noiembrie 2025 și septembrie 2026, media a coborât la 19,3 tone lunar, o reducere de aproximativ 75%.

Prin urmare, chiar dacă exporturile chinezești nu au fost oprite complet, accesul producătorilor americani la aceste materiale rămâne mult mai limitat decât înainte de declanșarea disputei comerciale.

Datele comerciale indică și faptul că restricțiile nu au afectat toate țările în aceeași măsură. În primele zece luni după acordul de la Busan, exporturile totale chinezești de materiale rare vizate de restricții au scăzut cu doar 2,5% față de perioada precedentă. În schimb, livrările cumulate către Statele Unite și Japonia au scăzut cu aproximativ 58%. În aceeași perioadă, exporturile către restul lumii au crescut cu aproximativ 146%. Astfel, Beijingul pare să fi păstrat un control considerabil asupra destinațiilor livrărilor, chiar dacă volumul total al exporturilor a rămas relativ stabil.

Japonia a fost afectată în mod deosebit. Exporturile chinezești de materiale rare către această țară au scăzut cu aproximativ 68% în perioada noiembrie 2025 – august 2026, comparativ cu cele zece luni precedente. Reducerea a venit inclusiv după ce Beijingul a impus noi restricții comerciale asupra Japoniei, în ianuarie 2026, pe fondul tensiunilor diplomatice legate de declarațiile premierului Sanae Takaichi privind posibilitatea unei intervenții japoneze în cazul unui atac chinez asupra Taiwanului.

Administrația Trump încearcă să accelereze dezvoltarea unei industrii americane a mineralelor critice, însă numeroase proiecte vor deveni operaționale abia la sfârșitul acestui deceniu sau chiar în următorul.

O rafinărie de 7,4 miliarde de dolari din Tennessee, susținută de compania sud-coreeană Korea Zinc, este programată să înceapă activitatea în 2030. Un proiect minier de cupru dezvoltat de Rio Tinto și BHP în America de Nord ar putea deveni operațional abia în următorul deceniu. De asemenea, compania Trilogy Metals intenționează să înceapă producția de cupru în Alaska în 2031.

Există și proiecte mai avansate, explică analiștii. MP Materials își extinde producția de magneți din pământuri rare în Texas, în cadrul unui parteneriat de mai multe miliarde de dolari cu Pentagonul. Mina Thacker Pass din Nevada, considerată cea mai mare sursă de litiu din America de Nord, este în construcție, iar producția este estimată să înceapă în 2028. În Idaho, Perpetua Resources intenționează să înceapă producția de antimoniu, utilizat inclusiv la fabricarea muniției și a blindajelor, în 2029.

Compania Vulcan Elements a început deja să producă magneți din pământuri rare în Carolina de Nord, însă produsele sale nu au primit încă toate aprobările necesare din partea clienților industriali. Problema Statelor Unite nu este, așadar, doar lipsa unor mine. China a construit în ultimele decenii o infrastructură complexă de rafinare și procesare, precum și expertiza tehnică necesară transformării materiilor prime în componente utilizabile de industrie. Dezvoltarea unor capacități similare presupune investiții foarte mari și perioade îndelungate.

În plus, strategia Administrației Trump se confruntă și cu obstacole politice interne. “Heat pumps are already delivering emissions cuts and protection from fossil fuel prices.”

Heat pumps can cut a quarter of the European Union’s energy emissions, as leaders are urged to “stop fiddling while the world burns and do what works”.

New analysis from the European Heat Pump Association (EHPA) found that fitting heat pumps in every building and “compatible industrial process” – powered by renewables like solar and wind – would avoid around 600 million tonnes (Mt) of CO2.

This is more than the annual emissions of Germany, the bloc’s biggest economy, or the 17 smallest EU countries combined.

What are heat pumps and how do they lower emissions?

Depending on the type, heat pumps work by capturing energy from air, water or the ground and turning it into heat or cold air – rather than burning fossil fuels on-site.

They work in a similar way to a refrigerator but in reverse, using a liquid chemical that turns into a hot gas through compression.

This hot gas releases its heat to your central heating, warming your home. The gas then cools down, turning back into liquid form, ready to start all over again.

For every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume, they typically deliver three to four kWh of heat.

According to EHPA, each residential heat pump installed displaces around 1,100 m3 of gas and two tonnes of CO2 per year on average, if the small amount of electricity it uses to run is from renewable sources.

There are already around 30 million residential heat pumps installed in Europe, with around three million added in 2025. This is one million fewer installations than the four million target set out by the European Commission.

Heat pump technology has become enmeshed in a “wave of misinformation” surrounding their ability to work in cold temperatures, their noise, and whether they can be installed in old buildings.

Euronews Earth has already debunked these myths here.

‘Climate change does not wait’

“Leaders need to stop fiddling while the world burns and do what works,” says Paul Kenny, director general of EHPA. “Heat pumps are already delivering emissions cuts and protection from fossil fuel prices.”

Kenny urged nations to make it easier to install heat pumps in every building and low temperature industry by ensuring upfront support, affordable, clean electricity and a “smooth” grid connection.

“Climate change does not wait and nor should we,” he adds.

From London’s iconic illuminated streets to the Capitale de Noël Strasbourg, explore the European cities where Christmas lights turn winter evenings into something magical.

As winter settles in across Europe, destinations are preparing to light up the festive season with dazzling streets and illuminated historical landmarks.

Some displays follow centuries-old traditions, while others use bold contemporary design and large-scale installations to bring a new look to the festivities.

Many of the displays are free to enjoy, making them an accessible way to experience a winter city break during the colder months.

Where to go in Europe to see Christmas lights

Copenhagen, Denmark

Christmas comes early at the Tivoli Gardens in Copenhagen – well, sort of. Running now until 3 January, the Danish capital’s amusement park takes on a festive makeover for Christmas, with thousands of twinkling lights, illuminated trees, decorations, seasonal food stalls and plenty of rides.

Ghent, Belgium

Ghent offers an atmospheric Christmas with a medieval centre that looks its best after dark. Illuminated dragons hang above bridges, their reflections shimmering in the canals below. The market winds through the old town with more than 150 wooden chalets, framed by the towers of St Bavo's Cathedral, the Belfry and Sint-Niklaaskerk. After exploring the market, visit the moated Gravensteen castle or join a chocolate tour.

Ljubljana, Slovenia

In Ljubljana, Christmas comes with a story as stars, crystals and abstract patterns shimmer above the streets and squares of the old town. This year’s theme, “Chaos. In order”, invites visitors to look up and spot the patterns hidden within "apparent disorder". The displays will be on from 27 November to 14 January. For a different view, take a boat ride along the river and watch the city’s famous bridges glow from the water.

London, England

London comes alive at Christmas and its best displays are scattered across the city, each with a character of its own. This year, Carnaby Street has brought a 1990s theme to Soho, while Regent Street’s famous glowing angels spread their wings above the traffic. Covent Garden shines with gold bells, giant baubles and more than 300,000 lights. Beyond the classic locations, head to Kensington to see "London's most Christmassy pub", the Churchill Arms, which is covered in real conifers and thousands of lights.

Málaga, Spain

Christmas in Málaga brings mild winter sunshine, and Calle Larios will light up for the festive season on 27 November. Away from the city centre, La Concepción Botanical Gardens will glow with a light trail themed “Christmas in the Garden of Oz”. Hunt for handmade ceramics and nativity figures at the markets, and look out for the city’s various nativity scenes, including the huge display at City Hall.

Munich, Germany

In Munich, the Christmas lights are at their most atmospheric on Marienplatz, where a towering tree glows against the Gothic façade of the New Town Hall. The tree is lit for the first time on 20 November, as the Christkindlmarkt opens, and you can browse the wooden stalls with a mug of Glühwein in hand.

Paris, France

Start at the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, where you can look down the Champs-Élysées at two long rows of trees wrapped in Christmas lights. The avenue’s illuminations run from 22 November to 4 January, and its Christmas market returns this year after a decade away. Over on Boulevard Haussmann, stop at Galeries Lafayette to see the Christmas windows designed by French fashion designer Jean-Charles de Castelbajac. Step inside to see the department store’s giant Christmas tree beneath its stained-glass dome, then head along the boulevard to Printemps for its knitting-themed window displays.

Prague, Czechia

Christmas in Prague, the City of a Hundred Spires, looks like a storybook come to life. In Old Town Square, the stalls gather beneath the astronomical clock, so you can warm up with a chimney cake while horse-drawn carriages roll past and music drifts from the stage. Climb the Old Town Hall tower for views over the Christmas market, then head to Charles Bridge at dusk to see the lamplighter during Advent.

Riga, Latvia

Picture a fairy tale where the streets are cobbled, the air smells of mulled wine, and lights glow beneath a medieval skyline – that is Riga at Christmas. In the Old Town, strings of lights hang above the wooden stalls in Dome Square, where the city’s Christmas tree stands beside the cathedral.

Strasbourg, France

Strasbourg's Christmas market has been running since 1570, making it the oldest in France and earning the city its title of the “Capitale de Noël”. Each December, facades, windows and balconies glow with light, and the scent of cinnamon and mulled wine drifts through the streets. A giant Christmas tree lights up Place Kléber, while hundreds of wooden chalets fill streets and squares across the city centre.

Tallinn, Estonia

In Tallinn, Christmas begins beneath the towering tree in Town Hall Square, where wooden stalls fan out across the cobblestones and the air smells of glögi and fresh gingerbread. The tree lighting takes place on 20 November and the Town Hall Square market runs until 6 January. After dark, follow a lantern tour through the narrow streets and then finish with a spin on the Old Town Ice Rink on Harju Street.

Vienna, Austria

Christmas feels like a waltz in Vienna: Elegant, unhurried and set against some of Europe's grandest streets. Illuminated chandeliers hang above the Graben, Kohlmarkt glows gold, and Kärntner Straße sparkles. Each Christmas market has its own personality, from the lively crowds at Rathausplatz to the smaller, prettier market at Belvedere.

Zürich, Switzerland

In Zürich, Christmas arrives on Bahnhofstrasse, where thousands of shimmering light crystals hang above the shopping street. The display, called “Lucy” after The Beatles’ song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds", runs from 19 November to 4 January. Stroll towards the lake and you will pass sparkling shop windows. At the Wienachtsdorf, one the city’s largest Christmas markets, stalls offer handmade gifts and local delicacies, and a warm fondue in the chalet is the perfect way to end the evening.

Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece are in the final stages of negotiations with Kigali’s government. The first pilot project could be announced on Monday and become operational in mid-2027, amid controversy over respect for fundamental rights and compatibility with EU law.

Rwanda will host the first-ever EU return hub built outside the bloc, in an unprecedented move to send irregular migrants to countries with which they have no connection.

The agreement between Kigali’s government and five EU member states is set to be announced on Monday in Vienna, after months of negotiations, two people familiar with the matter told Euronews.

The group of migration hardliners comprises Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece.

Their interior and migration ministers are attending a conference in the Austrian capital, where they will be joined by Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta. A few metres from the venue, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen will hold a press conference in the afternoon to announce the deal.

According to the sources, the first hub would be a “pilot project”, set to host a few hundred people deported from the five EU countries, starting in spring or summer 2027.

It would consist of open facilities housing migrants, who would receive a residence permit and be free to move around the country, with the aim of integrating them into local society and the labour market.

In principle, return hubs are temporary accommodation for migrants awaiting deportation to their countries of origin. However, there is no time limit on stays, and those involved could end up stranded in Rwanda and never be sent home.

The EU border agency Frontex could also be involved in deportations to Rwanda once the European Parliament and member states approve a reform of its mandate, recently proposed by the European Commission.

Rwanda's return hub may face legal challenges

Return hubs have raised concerns in Europe over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights. Critics warn they could lead to violations, particularly when established in countries with limited democratic standards.

The law enabling EU states to set up return hubs outside the bloc establishes that only non-EU countries — “where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law are respected” — are eligible.

According to the UN, Rwanda has a questionable track record of respect for human rights.

A similar agreement between Kigali and the United Kingdom, under which Britain would send asylum seekers to Rwanda, was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court in 2023 because of the risk of human rights abuses.

The five governments said the project would comply fully with EU law and international obligations, and would be run in partnership with international organisations such as the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

However, UNHCR and IOM are not directly involved in the negotiations on the procedures and could pull out if certain conditions are not met.

“IOM’s support requires a formal request from the receiving government, and assurances that adequate safeguards are in place,” a spokesperson for the organization told Euronews.

Legal complications may arise when deportations to Rwanda begin next year, as the European Court of Human Rights prohibits countries from transferring individuals to states or situations where they may face violations of fundamental rights.

“With this system, migrants may be subjected to torture and inhuman or degrading treatment,” Eleonora Celoria from Asgi, an Italian association of legal experts specialized in migration, told Euronews.

Costs are unclear

The five EU countries will bear the entire financial burden of the deportations and of accommodation in Rwanda.

There are no current estimates of the total costs, and it is unclear what Kigali will get in return. In 2025, the Rwandan government signed an agreement to accept third-country nationals expelled from the US in exchange for roughly $7.5 million in financial support.

A similar project set up by Italy in Albania sparked controversy over its costs, with a total bill of €670 million over a five-year partnership. According to a study from an Italian university, detaining migrants in these centres is much more expensive for Italy than hosting them on its own territory.

Each available place in Albania costs over €153,000, whereas comparable facilities in Sicily could accommodate migrants for approximately €21,000 per place.

More EU countries may join Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece in deporting irregular migrants to unrelated countries in the future.

Nineteen of the EU’s 27 governments are convinced this is an “innovative solution” for migration management, as a joint letter sent to EU leaders last June made clear.

Other countries, such as Spain and France, have rebuked the deportation scheme, setting themselves on a collision course with a growing political majority within the EU.

Ahead of European markets opening, Asian stocks mostly fell on Monday as the tech sector struggled to recover from the crisis at Nvidia after boss Jensen Huang stepped down, with the company's earnings this week and market debut of Anthropic keeping the AI trade in focus.

Investors will also be keeping close tabs on geopolitical developments, with Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin holding their first trilateral summit on the sidelines of the APEC gathering.

AI-linked firms continued to fall in early exchanges as the fallout from the upheaval at Nvidia courses through trading floors.

Huang, a pivotal figure in the artificial intelligence boom, resigned Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The 63-year-old's departure raised concerns about the chip titan, which is at the centre of a buildout that has helped propel global markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the world.

The day looked set for a positive start after the Financial Times reported that Huang was in talks for a spectacular return to the hotseat, while several Silicon Valley titans have backed calls for his return.

Tycoon Elon Musk and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick were among the more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter demanding the firm's board to "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts".

However, the report did not appear to be having much of an impact in Asia, with Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei - home to most of the region's AI-linked firms - all well down.

Among the hardest-hit companies were Japan's Kioxia and Tokyo Electron as well as Taiwan giant TSMC and SK hynix of South Korea.

There were also losses in Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Manila and Jakarta.

"After the bombshells dropped on markets last week, investors have had the weekend to digest the developments and reassess risk with a clearer mind," wrote Chris Weston at Pepperstone.

"That said, I'm not convinced we're any closer to pricing the future with a new sense of conviction.

"We'll see whether the reinstatement trade can gather momentum," he added.

However, he said "even if Huang were to return, alleviating the immediate key-man risk, the prospect of tighter governance requirements and additional political or regulatory constraints would remain a significant overhang".

Nvidia is due to report its earnings on Tuesday, giving a fresh view on the outlook for the AI trade, while the listing of Anthropic - creator of the Claude chatbot - will provide some insight into investors' AI sentiment.

The Xi-Trump-Putin meeting on the sidelines of APEC in southern China will be closely watched, but it is unclear whether the wars in Iran and Ukraine, which have sent energy prices soaring, will be on the agenda.

Oil prices edged down after the International Energy Agency last week said global supplies were expected to exceed demand in the fourth quarter, though that was offset by Iran claiming an attack on a US military base in Bahrain at the weekend.

It comes after a network failure triggered a rare nationwide grounding of all planes on Friday.

The Trump administration is pushing Congress for $50 billion to overhaul the United States’ ageing air traffic control system after a network failure triggered a rare nationwide grounding of all planes on Friday.

Thousands of flights were halted, and passengers across the US are still struggling to reach their destinations as investigators say they are working to establish exactly what went wrong.

Silent on the grounding for two days, President Donald Trump on Sunday broke his silence on his social media platform Truth Social, saying Congress should approve the money “desperately needed” for the system, which he called “RIDICULOUS” for being 50 years old.

Congress approved $12.5 billion (10.95 billion euros) in 2025 to modernise the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)'s systems, some of which date to the 1960s. The first phase is due for completion by December 2028.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told lawmakers in September that a second phase would cost at least $10 billion (€8.7 billion) more, and a September bill from Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt sought about $30 billion in new investment.

Democrats say they want answers on how existing funds have been spent and why the request has grown.

What caused the network failure?

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Friday said he wants $50 billion for air traffic control and said he would send lawmakers a detailed request on Monday.

According to Duffy, Friday's problem began when a federal contractor replaced a section of old copper wire with fibre cable at a site in El Dorado, Arkansas. When the router was switched on, a fault emerged at a facility in Amarillo, Texas, cascading into the ground stop.

The FAA said “excessive data” flooded the system at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilising aircraft communications and radar feeds. The network stabilised after the contractor blocked the two locations.

Duffy said officials are “pretty good” that the outage was not a cyberattack, as intelligence agencies have not detected the “chatter or the footprints” they would expect to see.

Duffy, who appeared on five Sunday talk shows, said the funds are needed to build a “brand new architecture” for the network. He said telecoms firms including AT&T, Verizon and Lumen could deploy it “tomorrow” if funding were in place.

Pushing back, Democrats say they back an upgrade but are questioning the price tag. Those on the House Transportation Committee say most of the money appropriated last year remains unspent.

“Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?” said Rep. Rick Larsen, the committee’s ranking Democrat, and Rep. André Carson in a joint statement. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said Congress has already shown it is willing to invest.

The dispute previews the sharper scrutiny the administration is likely to face when Democrats take control of Congress in January.

According to Duffy, operations should be at full capacity by Monday, but travellers heading to or connecting through the US should check with their airline for rebookings, as backlogs may take time to clear.

The US operates the world’s busiest airspace, with the FAA handling roughly 45,000 flights a day, making a nationwide ground stop potentially disrupt connections and long-haul schedules far beyond American airports.

“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Pope Leo said, to applause from a crowd many of whom wore the feathered headdresses and face markings of the region.

Pope Leo XIV on Sunday demanded justice for environmental defenders killed while protecting the Amazon and backed Indigenous communities fighting to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging, illegal mining and what he called an “insatiable thirst for domination”.

On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo travelled into the Peruvian rainforest and echoed a central teaching of Pope Francis: that care for the most vulnerable and care for creation cannot be separated.

“The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” he told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered on the Ucayali River in Pucallpa, in Peru’s northeast.

He said he had come to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to the 57 murders of environmental defenders that campaign groups estimate took place between 2010 and 2024.

The visit to Cusco, 3,400 metres (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues his recovering from lung cancer surgery last month.

A call for a different model of development

Drawing on his years as a bishop in Peru and on Francis’ constant preaching on the environment and Indigenous peoples, Leo used the encounter and a Mass that followed to call for an economic model that respects the Earth and those who protect it, rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” practised by outsiders.

“Very little has been done — and very slowly at that — while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at Mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”

Illegal mining and coca production are also driving deforestation and encroaching on Indigenous territories, putting ancestral lands at risk and exposing communities to violence and organised crime.

On Saturday, Peruvian police reported three operations against illegal mining in Madre de Dios, one of the country’s most biodiverse regions, destroying equipment, rafts and engines valued at €3.8 million ($4.1 million).

In Peru, most killings of environmental defenders go unpunished, and convictions are rare. In 2025, the courts upheld 28-year prison sentences for four timber merchants over the murder of four Indigenous people who opposed logging, after a trial lasting a decade.

The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, ambushed and killed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region in 2023.

In August, a court sentenced four people to up to 35 years in prison. It found Inuma had filed a complaint against the defendants to stop deforestation and other crimes, including drug trafficking, and that they plotted his death because he had spoken out.

Sexual violence against Indigenous schoolgirls

Leo also addressed a sharp rise in sexual violence against Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in Condorcanqui province, in the northern Amazon, and condemned the “complicity”, “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding it.

The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council, Comuawuy, has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the province between January and July alone.

After persistent demands from women’s groups, specialised prosecutors’ offices were created and the government launched a prevention plan. In January, the Ministry of Women and Vulnerable Populations announced a 32-year prison sentence for a man accused of sexually abusing a 14-year-old girl.

The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.

Overall, the 71-year-old has appeared unfazed by the three-nation trip, the longest of his pontificate, which began on 6 November.

While others aboard the papal plane have fallen ill, Leo has shown no sign of fatigue and has seemed energised, particularly by the days spent seeing old friends in his former diocese of Chiclayo.

The Pope mostly sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.

After 150 years of Heinz ketchup, the brand’s European president reveals the secret behind its enduring appeal and how it keeps generations of customers coming back.

Did you know that food is the largest manufacturing industry in Europe?

Almost five million people are employed in food and drink manufacturing and it generates around €1.5 trillion of sales every year.

But what you might not realise is why it’s so important for our security, competitiveness and its influence across the world.

In this episode of The Big Question, Angela Barnes is joined in the studio by Willem Brandt, president for Europe and Pacific developed markets at Kraft Heinz to discuss why Europe is so important to the food industry.

“You're only ever three missed meals away from a revolution”

It’s not clear who said the original quote, with some attributing versions to American journalist Alfred Henry Lewis and many miscredits to soviet revolutionary Vladimir Lenin, but the point still stands. Here, Willem referenced it to denote the precarious nature of modern security and economies.

“If you look at the whole European geopolitical situation, you see that policymakers here really care about security and they really care a lot about competitiveness,” Willem explained.

“And food sits right at the heart of both of those things in Europe if you ask me, because ultimately, we've got a very good and strong value chain with farmers and industry and retailers, but we've gotta keep it that way to make sure that we keep the food on our plates going forward as well.”

In order to keep the food industry thriving for all players, Willem urged policymakers to reduce fragmentation across the bloc to ensure the highest standards for all consumers, but also insisted a cap on unfair trading practices should be removed.

This directive is intended to protect small producers, like farmers, against a number of black- and grey-listed activities, such as short notice cancellations on perishable agri-food products, and delayed payments. However, the cap only protects companies with turnovers of less than €350 million and Willem argued that fairness should apply to all, regardless of size.

What trends are shaping the food industry right now?

While the food industry may be bolstering the European economy, it’s also shaping the industry globally too.

“Food really matters here and Europe matters to food,” Willem told The Big Question.

He went on to explain how Europe is shaping food trends by developing and testing new product categories before rolling them out more widely, with health increasingly influencing consumer preferences.

“Forty percent of consumers in Europe are trying to cut back on sugar,” he explained.

Adding that one of their biggest hits right now is ketchup with zero added salt and sugar. It’s seen a 26% growth and over half of that is reportedly from new customers, people who previously didn’t purchase ketchup at all.

“And that's now travelled across the globe. So it's launched in Brazil now. There, even 80% of the buyers didn't buy ketchup before, so that's really meeting the consumers where they are.”

He said this philosophy is central to Kraft Heinz’s long-term success. As the brand celebrates 150 years of its iconic tomato ketchup, Willem explained that its enduring appeal lies in striking the right balance between consistency and evolution.

While the product has retained its familiar taste and identity across generations, it has also adapted to changing consumer preferences, with the introduction of organic, zero-sugar and flavoured varieties over the years.

“There's still phenomenal growth for brands like that,” Willem told The Big Question.

He also highlighted the importance of striking the right balance between quality and affordability. With household budgets under pressure, consumers are increasingly price-conscious but are still reluctant to compromise on quality.

“If you want that quality you've got to control the entire chain, which is why we have our own seeds department who really continuously work on the seeds that we use for our own tomatoes,” he added.

“Then there's really the long-term partnerships with the growers and the farmers that leads to better yields on the farmland and of course, we've got our proprietary recipe which is a very well kept secret and our own manufacturing processes. So doing the whole end-to-end chain is what makes Heinz ketchup so delicious and so good.”

Carney's remarks come days before a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, where auto manufacturing is expected to be on the agenda.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Ottawa could look to Chinese automakers if negotiations with US President Donald Trump fail to safeguard an integrated North American car industry.

Speaking to reporters at the Francophonie Summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, on Monday, Carney said Canada’s auto workers, which he called “the best in the world”, should be “fully deployed” in a continental market. That market, he said, “has become less integrated because of US trade actions”.

He insisted that talks with the United States remain his priority but said their outcome could determine whether Ottawa turns to European, Chinese or Japanese manufacturers instead.

Asked whether the prospect of Chinese investment was a bargaining chip in the US talks, he answered, "It's not leverage. But action, reaction.”

“If they’re not fully utilised in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” he said of Canada’s auto workers and factories. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

His remarks come days before a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, where auto manufacturing is expected to be on the agenda.

Earlier, Carney in Manila on Saturday said that any trade deal with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He stressed that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two sides were making progress towards a possible agreement, though differences remained.

Carney states conditions for Chinese investment

Carney was clear that any Chinese involvement would have to go well beyond assembly. Investment would need to include substantial manufacturing in Canada, proper labour standards, and domestic supply chains that grow over time, including the use of Canadian critical minerals in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Carney and Xi reached an agreement in January that cut Canada’s 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%. The deal initially allows up to 49,000 vehicles a year, with the cap set to rise over time. In return, Beijing agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural goods, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the arrangement to draw Chinese investment into Canada’s car industry and create jobs.

The agreement was criticised by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the heart of Canadian auto manufacturing. Ford warned it could threaten Canadian jobs and put access to the US market at risk.

Canada’s auto sector depends heavily on cross-border production. The “Detroit Three” of Ford, General Motors and Stellantis run plants across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders several times before a vehicle is finished. Trump has repeatedly pressed carmakers to shift production from Canada to the US.

His tariffs have disrupted the industry. Canada recently threatened legal action against Stellantis after the company moved planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.
